lead: Real machine parts rarely carry one kind of stress. A shaft with a pulley is bent and twisted at the same point; a bracket with an offset load is pulled and bent at once. At a point, the stresses from each load add (superposition) into one stress state, and that state is then turned to find the principal stresses: the largest and smallest normal stresses at the point, on planes that carry no shear. They tell where a brittle part will crack and feed the failure theories for ductile parts. Some syllabi call this the calculation of principal stresses for various load combinations.
prereq: You need the stress formulas of direct, bending and torsional stresses.

blocks.text: Superposition holds while the material stays linear elastic and the deflections are small. Take a small square element at the chosen point. The face whose normal is the x-axis carries a normal stress σ<sub>x</sub> and a shear stress τ<sub>xy</sub>; the y face carries σ<sub>y</sub> and the same τ<sub>xy</sub>. Tension is positive.
σx = ±P/A ± My/I; τxy = Tr/J (+ shear from V)

P/A, My/I and Tr/J are the direct, bending and torsional stresses at that point, each with the sign it has there. For a solid shaft at its surface, σ<sub>x</sub> = 32M/(πd³) and τ<sub>xy</sub> = 16T/(πd³); σ<sub>y</sub> = 0, so the element is in plane stress.

Pick the point where the stresses add: the outer fibre on the side where bending and direct stress have the same sign. Transverse shear from V is zero at that outer fibre and largest at the neutral axis, so it is checked separately in short, deep members.

sections.h3: Eccentric loading: a force plus a moment

blocks.text: An eccentric load is a force whose line of action misses the centroid of the section by a distance e. Moving it to the centroid keeps the force and adds a couple M = Pe. The section then carries a uniform direct stress P/A and a linear bending stress Pe·c/I; they add on one side and subtract on the other.

P is the load (N), e its offset from the centroidal axis (mm), c the distance from the neutral axis to the outer fibre (mm) and I the second moment of area about the axis of bending (mm⁴). If the load is offset in two directions, add the two bending stresses at the corner where they have the same sign.

The rule applies to brackets, clamps, columns with offset loads and the straight parts of C-frames; never use P/A alone when the force is offset. Bolted and welded joints under eccentric loads are treated in their own chapters.

Rotate the element by an angle θ and the stresses on its faces change. On two perpendicular planes the shear stress is zero; these are the principal planes and their normal stresses are the principal stresses σ₁ (algebraically larger) and σ₂.

The square root is also the maximum in-plane shear stress τ<sub>max</sub> = (σ₁ − σ₂)/2, which acts on planes at 45° to the principal planes. The principal planes are at θ<sub>p</sub> from the x face, where tan 2θ<sub>p</sub> = 2τ<sub>xy</sub>/(σ<sub>x</sub> − σ<sub>y</sub>). Check: σ₁ + σ₂ = σ<sub>x</sub> + σ<sub>y</sub>.

Mohr's circle draws the same result. Plot the x face as the point (σx, τxy) and the y face as (σy, −τxy); the line joining them is a diameter. The centre is at ((σx + σy)/2, 0) and the radius is τmax. The circle cuts the σ axis at σ₁ and σ₂, and an angle 2θ on the circle is θ on the element. Figure 1.7.1 draws the circle of the first worked example.

In plane stress the third principal stress, normal to the surface, is σ₃ = 0. When σ₁ and σ₂ have the same sign, the largest shear stress at the point is σ₁/2 (or |σ₂|/2), larger than the in-plane value. A brittle part is checked by comparing σ₁ with its allowable tensile stress; a ductile part needs a theory of failure (maximum shear stress or distortion energy), covered with failure theories and fatigue design.

examples.question: A 50 mm diameter solid shaft transmits 15 kW at 300 rpm and carries a bending moment of 800 N·m at the section considered. Find the bending and torsional stresses at the surface, the principal stresses, the maximum shear stress and the angle of the principal planes.
steps: Centre and radius: (65.19 + 0)/2 = 32.60 MPa; τ<sub>max</sub> = √(32.60² + 19.45²) = 37.96 MPa.
Principal stresses: σ₁ = 32.60 + 37.96 = 70.55 MPa; σ₂ = 32.60 − 37.96 = −5.36 MPa. Check: 70.55 − 5.36 = 65.19 = σ<sub>x</sub> + σ<sub>y</sub>.
Angle: tan 2θ<sub>p</sub> = 2 × 19.45/65.19 = 0.597, so 2θ<sub>p</sub> = 30.8° and θ<sub>p</sub> = 15.4° from the shaft axis.
examples.answer: σ<sub>x</sub> = 65.19 MPa, τ<sub>xy</sub> = 19.45 MPa; σ₁ = 70.55 MPa, σ₂ = −5.36 MPa, τ<sub>max</sub> = 37.96 MPa; principal planes at 15.4° (and 105.4°) from the shaft axis.

examples.question: A tie bar 40 mm wide and 10 mm thick carries a pull of 20 kN whose line of action is 15 mm from the centroidal axis, in the plane of the width. Find the largest and smallest normal stresses.
steps: Area A = 40 × 10 = 400 mm². Direct stress P/A = 20,000/400 = 50.0 MPa (tension).
Moment M = Pe = 20,000 × 15 = 300,000 N·mm, bending about the axis normal to the width.
Edge nearer the load: 50.0 + 112.5 = 162.5 MPa tension. Far edge: 50.0 − 112.5 = −62.5 MPa, compression.
There is no shear at the edges, so these are principal stresses there.
examples.answer: σ<sub>max</sub> = 162.5 MPa (tension) on the edge nearer the load line and σ<sub>min</sub> = −62.5 MPa (compression) on the far edge: the offset raises the stress 3.25 times above P/A.

traps: Adding a shear stress to a normal stress. Combine them only through the principal-stress formula or Mohr's circle.
Forgetting the moment Pe of an offset load: P/A alone can be several times too small (162.5 against 50 MPa in the tie bar).
Dropping the sign of σ₂. A negative principal stress is compression and matters for brittle parts and for the maximum shear stress.
Reading 2θ off Mohr's circle as θ on the element. The angle on the circle is twice the angle on the element.
Checking a ductile part by σ₁ alone. Ductile materials yield in shear; use a theory of failure.

quiz.q: Define principal planes and principal stresses.
quiz.a: Principal planes are the planes at a point that carry no shear stress; the normal stresses on them are the principal stresses.

quiz.q: State the centre and radius of Mohr's circle for plane stress.
Why does an eccentric axial load give both direct and bending stress?
quiz.a: Moving the force to the centroid keeps the force (uniform P/A) and adds a couple M = Pe, which bends the section (linear Pe·c/I).

quiz.q: At a point σ<sub>x</sub> = 100 MPa, σ<sub>y</sub> = 40 MPa and τ<sub>xy</sub> = 30 MPa. Find σ₁, σ₂ and τ<sub>max</sub>.
quiz.a: Centre 70 MPa; radius √(30² + 30²) = 42.43 MPa; σ₁ = 112.43 MPa, σ₂ = 27.57 MPa, in-plane τ<sub>max</sub> = 42.43 MPa (both principal stresses are tensile, so the largest shear at the point is 112.43/2 = 56.2 MPa).

quiz.q: A 40 mm solid shaft carries M = 500 N·m and T = 300 N·m. Find σ₁ and σ₂ at the surface.
The 40 mm shaft of the direct-stress chapter has −119.36 MPa normal stress and 35.81 MPa shear on its compression side. Find the principal stresses there.
quiz.a: Centre −59.68 MPa; radius √(59.68² + 35.81²) = 69.60 MPa; σ₁ = 9.92 MPa, σ₂ = −129.28 MPa, τ<sub>max</sub> = 69.60 MPa.

quiz.q: At the neutral axis of a shaft under bending and torsion, the bending stress is zero. What are the principal stresses there?
quiz.a: Pure shear: σ₁ = +τ, σ₂ = −τ, on planes at 45° to the axis, and τ<sub>max</sub> = τ.

beyond: Strain-gauge rosettes measure three strains on a surface and give the principal stresses of a real part by the same transformation. Finite element programs report principal and von Mises stresses at every node, and fatigue software searches for the critical plane. Search next for strain rosette analysis, three-dimensional Mohr's circles and von Mises stress.
